items.title: Today's lesson
items.content:
A doctor listening to a **heartbeat** and a tall **coconut palm** open the lesson: how do food, oxygen and water reach every part of a large body?

Students trace blood through the **four chambers** of the heart, compare a fish's, a frog's and a bird's heart to see why **double circulation** matters, and compare the three kinds of **blood vessels** with platelets and lymph.

Water is followed up the **xylem** and food through the **phloem**, back to the coconut.

Some pictures have a **second picture or animation**: show picture 1, ask, then click ›.

items.title: You already know
items.content:
• blood has plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets

• oxygen enters the blood in the alveoli; haemoglobin carries it

• digested food is absorbed into the blood in the villi

• xylem and phloem are the conducting tissues of plants; stomata let water vapour out

items.title: By the end, you can
items.content:
**1.** Describe the structure of the human heart and trace blood flow through it.

**2.** Explain double circulation and why it matters in birds and mammals.

**3.** Compare arteries, veins and capillaries, and state the roles of platelets and lymph.

**4.** Explain transport in plants: water through xylem (transpiration pull) and food through phloem (translocation).

**5.** Label a diagram of the human heart.

items.text:
**Step 1: start here**

Read the key idea: diffusion is too slow in a large body, so **blood** carries materials and the **heart** pumps it. Then reveal the heart (pointer 2).

**Step 2: picture 1 of 2**

The heart cut open. The four **chamber names are hidden** (?). Point to the two upper and two lower chambers.

**Answer to Question 3**

**Step 3. Four**: two **atria** above (they receive blood) and two **ventricles** below (they pump blood out).

**Step 4: click › (now 2 of 2)**

After Question 3: the chamber names appear: right atrium, left atrium, right ventricle, left ventricle.

**Answer to Question 4**

**Step 5.** The **left ventricle**: it pumps blood to the **whole body**. The right ventricle pumps only to the nearby lungs; the atria push blood just into the ventricles below them.

**Answer to Question 5**

**Step 6.** The right side carries **carbon-dioxide-rich** blood and the left side **oxygen-rich** blood; keeping them apart sends the most oxygen to the body.

**Answer to Question 6**

**Step 7.** Blood would be pushed **back into the atrium**. Valves (labelled on the figure) let blood flow only one way; the “lub-dub” is the sound of valves closing. Question 1 from the hook is now answered.

items.prompt: In this heart, which chamber pumps blood to the whole body?
What stops blood from flowing back into an atrium when its ventricle contracts?

items.text:
**On this question**

**A**: **F**, the left ventricle, which has the thickest wall. All the parts: A vena cava, B pulmonary artery, C right atrium, D aorta, E left atrium, F left ventricle.

**On this question**

**A**: the **valves** between each atrium and its ventricle let blood flow only one way.

**Step 1: picture 1, then click ›**

Picture 1: the path of blood through the heart, lungs and body. Trace it with the class while reading the key idea (pointer 2).

**Step 2**

Read the key idea, tracing each step on the figure, starting from the **lungs**.

**Step 3: now click ›**

Picture 2: one red blood cell starts at the **lungs**, just as the key idea does, and makes **one complete round**: red while oxygen-rich, blue after the body, with a caption for each step. It passes through the heart **twice**.

*Picture 2 is animated: it plays on its own and repeats. Click **‹** to return to picture 1 and stop it.*

**Step 4**

Read the key idea: the animation passed through the heart **twice**: this is **double circulation**. Next: is it the same in other animals?

items.text:
**Step 1: picture 1 of 3**

The **fish** heart: 2 chambers. Red = oxygen-rich blood, blue = carbon-dioxide-rich (legend below). Follow its blood with the class.

**Answer to Question 7**

**Step 2. Once**: heart → gills → body → heart. It picks up oxygen in the **gills**: **single circulation**.

**Step 3: click › (now 2 of 3)**

The **frog** heart appears: two atria, **one ventricle** (purple = mixed blood).

**Answer to Question 8**

**Step 4.** Oxygen-rich and carbon-dioxide-rich blood **mix** a little, so less oxygen reaches the body.

**Step 5: click › (now 3 of 3)**

The **bird or mammal** heart appears: four chambers, the two kinds of blood kept **completely apart**. Then read the key idea below.

**Step 6**

Read the key idea: why birds and mammals need four chambers.

items.prompt: Which is the correct path of a red blood cell? (VC: vena cava, RA: right atrium, RV: right ventricle, PA: pulmonary artery)
How many times does blood pass through the heart in one complete round in (i) a fish, (ii) a human?
**Assertion (A):** Birds and mammals need complete separation of oxygen-rich and carbon-dioxide-rich blood. **Reason (R):** They use a lot of energy to keep their body temperature constant.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A.
Both are true, but R does not explain A.
A is true, R is false.
A is false, R is true.

items.text:
**On this question**

**A**: vena cava → right atrium (RA) → right ventricle (RV) → pulmonary artery → lungs.

**On this question**

**A**: a fish has single circulation (**once**); we have double circulation (**twice**).

**On this question**

**(a)**: separation gives an efficient oxygen supply for their high energy needs.

items.text:
**Step 1: reveal (a) only**

The **artery**, labels hidden. Keep (b) and (c) hidden for now.

**Answer to Question 9**

**Step 2.** It is **thick, muscular and elastic**, so it does not burst and it stretches with each heartbeat.

**Step 3: click › on (a)**

The artery's labels appear: thick, muscular, elastic wall; narrow space.

**Step 4: reveal (b)**

The **vein**, labels hidden.

**Answer to Question 10**

**Step 5.** So blood flows **only towards the heart**, even upwards from the legs.

**Step 6: click › on (b)**

The vein's labels appear: thin wall, wide space, valve.

**Step 7: reveal (c)**

The **capillary**, labels hidden.

**Answer to Question 11**

**Step 8.** Materials must pass **through the wall** quickly; a wall only **one cell thick** lets food, oxygen and wastes diffuse across easily.

**Step 9: click › on (c)**

The capillary's labels appear: wall only one cell thick; red blood cells in single file.

**Step 10**

Read the key idea: capillaries join arteries to veins; vessels are named by **direction**, not oxygen.

items.prompt: Fill in the blanks: The blood vessel that brings oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the heart is the ______. Blood vessels with walls only one cell thick are ______.
A boy has a disorder in which his platelets are very few. Why is a small cut dangerous for him?
options: His cut gets infected at once

items.text:
**On this question**

**A**: **pulmonary vein**; **capillaries**. (B) The pulmonary artery carries blood to the lungs, not from them.

**On this question**

**A**: platelets help blood **clot**; with very few, the cut keeps bleeding.

items.text:
**Step 1: start here**

Read the key idea: plants use a slower system; **xylem** carries water, **phloem** carries food.

**Step 2: picture 1 only**

Water enters at the **root hairs**, rises in the **xylem**, and leaves the leaves as **water vapour** through the **stomata**. Do not click › yet.

**Answer to Question 12**

**Step 3.** The root has more ions than the soil, so water moves **into the root**, pushing a column of water up the xylem (**root pressure**).

**Answer to Question 13**

**Step 4.** The lost water is replaced from the xylem in the leaf, which **pulls** the whole water column up from the roots: **transpiration pull**. Then click › on the figure. Question 2 from the hook is now answered.

**Step 5: now click ›**

Picture 2: water vapour drifts off the leaves while water drops are pulled up the xylem from the roots.

*Picture 2 is animated: it plays on its own and repeats. Click **‹** to return to picture 1 and stop it.*

**Step 6**

Read the key idea: transpiration pull by **day**, root pressure at **night**.

**Step 1: picture 1 of 2**

A plant with its **xylem** and **phloem** in the stem. Which way each one carries materials is hidden for now.

**Step 2**

Read the key idea: **translocation** in the phloem, which uses energy.

**Answer to Question 14**

**Step 3. No**: xylem carries only **water and minerals**, and only **upwards**. Phloem moves food **up or down**, wherever it is needed. Then click › on the figure.

**Step 4: click › (now 2 of 2)**

After Question 14: the arrows appear. Xylem (blue): water and minerals, **up only**; phloem (orange): food, **up and down**.

items.prompt: On a hot, sunny, windy day, does water rise faster or more slowly in the xylem of a plant?
A ring of bark, which contains the phloem, is removed all round a tree's trunk. The leaves stay green for weeks, but the roots slowly die. Why?

items.text:
**On this question**

**A**: more water evaporates from the leaves, so the **transpiration pull** is stronger.

**On this question**

**A**: the xylem inside still carries water up, so the leaves survive; but **food** cannot pass the ring in the **phloem**, so the roots starve.
